lesson.title: September 11, 2001
lesson.summary: On the morning of September 11, 2001, al Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners and attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people in the deadliest terrorist attack in American history and setting the course of American foreign and domestic policy for years to come.
lesson.body:
On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen hijackers affiliated with the terrorist network al Qaeda took control of four commercial airplanes shortly after takeoff from airports on the East Coast. Two planes struck the twin towers of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan, causing both 110 story buildings to collapse within about two hours. A third plane struck the Pentagon, the headquarters of the U.S. Department of Defense, just outside Washington, D.C. The fourth plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew, aware of the other attacks through phone calls, fought to retake control of the cockpit. Investigators believe that plane's intended target was likely the U.S. Capitol or the White House. Nearly 3,000 people were killed that day, including hundreds of firefighters and police officers who had rushed into the towers to help evacuate them.

The attacks were planned and organized by al Qaeda, a militant Islamist network led by Osama bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi who had turned against the United States over its policies in the Middle East. A central grievance for bin Laden was the presence of American troops stationed in Saudi Arabia, home to Islam's holiest sites, ever since the buildup to the Gulf War in 1990 and 1991. What bin Laden and other al Qaeda leaders saw as an ongoing American military presence in the region, along with U.S. support for Israel and sanctions on Iraq, fed the grievances that led to the attacks.

The attacks also exposed how a small, loosely organized non state network could exploit the openness of a globalized, interconnected society, coordinating internationally, moving money quietly, and using ordinary tools like commercial flight training and email, to inflict catastrophic harm without the resources of a state military. That vulnerability, in which determined and creative adversaries could turn a country's own open networks and infrastructure against it, foreshadowed a broader set of anxieties in the years that followed about protecting not just airports and buildings but digital systems and infrastructure from equally determined and less visible attackers.

The scale of the attacks, unfolding live on television, produced a profound shock across American society and a wave of national unity. Within days, Congress authorized the use of military force against those responsible, and President George W. Bush's administration began building the policies, from a new Department of Homeland Security to sweeping surveillance laws to military action overseas, that would define what soon became known as the War on Terror.
